Situation1: There is a scheduled family gathering on the calendar.
Situation2: They notice swimmers occasionally entering the shallow area without supervision.
Story: I glanced at the calendar on my phone, a bright circle marking today’s family gathering. My daughter had called twice already, reminding me how much the grandkids were looking forward to our afternoon together. I could almost hear their laughter, feel their small hands tugging at mine, and I longed to be there, to be the grandparent who never missed a moment. But as I scanned the pool deck, my lifeguard instincts kicked in. A group of kids, unsupervised, darted into the shallow end, splashing and shrieking. I knew the rules—no one in the water without an adult. My supervisor expected vigilance, unwavering attention to every swimmer’s safety. The weight of both roles pressed on me: the promise to my family, the duty to these children. My heart tugged in two directions, torn between the warmth of family and the responsibility of keeping strangers safe. I stood at the edge, the whistle in my hand, caught in the tension of what I owed to those I loved and those who depended on me.
